items.text: Roaming through 1969

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: Joanna.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: It's open. Come in.
The mechanical woman enters her friend's house.
Joanna's Home, 1969

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: Did you move the TV upstairs?
She stands in a tidy living room, but there is no sign of her host.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: Yeah. The antenna's stuck. Michael couldn't fix it, so we brought it up here, where it could catch the signal.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: Come on up, Lucy. I'm trying to get this darned thing working. It won't take long, I promise.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: Are you in need of help?

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: It's okay. I'm almost done. It's just this screw. It won't get in there—don't make me get rough with you, you naughty garoto!
The mechanical woman sits down and looks at the clock. It is 4:11 in the afternoon. She can easily imagine how busy her colleagues are at the Space Center.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: They should be close to landing on the moon now.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: Yeah, close. I'm close to making it work. Done!
The wires spark and burn. It strikes the woman like mocking laughter.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: It appears to be broken.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: A simple adjustment will resolve this issue.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: Alrighty then! Let's grab something to eat first, and then we'll see what I can do, or I guess, what you can do.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: Would you like to try some pamonha? It's an old family recipe from Portugal.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: I do not need food to replenish energy, Joanna. But, thank you.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: Oh, I completely forgot, haha.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: But it can't hurt to have something to eat, right? You are capable of it after all. Anyways, it's your call.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: Biological material has a much lower conversion efficiency than pure electricity.
It had been a century since she had changed her primary power source. It had increased her capacity exponentially.
Yet it came with an unexpected price: she no longer felt welcome at meal times. Humans consider fuel consumption a social activity, and some take offense to her abstaining.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: Perhaps high-nutrient foods will become more popular in the future. That way, less time will be wasted on social consumption rituals.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: Oh please, food isn't just about the health of your body. It's good for your spirit too! It's one of the great joys of living.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: Irrelevant. Whatever a spirit is, it is not nourished by biological matter. Now, consider the food we prepared for the astronauts, lightweight but densely-packed with nutrients—

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: Fine, no pamonha for you. Now would you fix this machine? I don't want to miss the broadcast.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: Yes. It is possible. However, I must warn you, there is a small chance of failure. I predict between 2 to 5%.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: Well, I already called the repairman. But if you don't mind trying your luck, maybe you can give it a whirl first?
The mechanical woman reaches for the stubborn screw, and steam pours out from her core. The light of arcane skill seems to awaken the machine, and then ...
In a fit of sputtering smoke, the unlikeliest probability seems to have come to pass.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: *coughs* What's happening, Lucy?

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: My arcane skill has failed.
A finger-sized robot now stands motionless next to a piston where Lucy had been. The piston squeaks up to Joanna from the ground.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: It has been 42 months and 18 days since the last time this failure occurred.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: How unfortunate.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: Seems like we made a bad gamble, haha.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: But it isn't so bad. Why, you almost look like a little dolly now. Very, very cute, Miss Lucy.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: But, how do you get back to your usual size?

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: It will be over in just a few minutes. Do not be concerned.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: I never expected to learn something new about you after all these years.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: I am no more than a metal piston truly. Everything else is just a mechanical construction. A facade.
She looks now just as she did when she was first awakened.
When she took form as a part of that very first steam engine.
A few seconds pass, and Joanna picks up the tiny, immobile robot.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: I still can't believe this little thing was you.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: An accident caused by a rare instability with my arcane skill.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: I suppose you see now why I am reluctant to use my skills, even when they are important. It is dangerous to bet on an uncertainty.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: Thankfully it's only a TV this time. Not that big a deal, right? Besides, it was only a tiny, little accident. You can always try again.
Once again, Lucy emits steam from her core, this time successfully reactivating the television with her arcane skill.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: Done.
A signal reaches the TV from 300,000 kilometers away. On the black-and-white screen, a man begins to step out from a capsule, his feet landing on the surface of the moon.
The camera captures not only the capsule and the astronaut, but the silence and loneliness of space.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: It looks so beautiful up there.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: In some many different cultures, people believed something was living on the moon. In China, they say there's a palace on the moon, with a princess and a rabbit.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: There is no breathable atmosphere on the moon. Such a thing would be logically impossible.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: Well, we're about to see. They're taking the first steps now.
It may only be one small step for man, but for mankind, it is a journey of many thousand years.
She watches as the astronauts take their first clumsy steps across the moonscape.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: It was less than 70 years, Joanna, when most people believed humanity would never fly. And now, you have taken the first step on another world.
Joanna is still silent in awe of the moment, but in a short while, she points over to a painting on the wall.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: That painting was from Uncle Victor.
A painting that has kept her company throughout her life.
Depicted on it, a winged girl taking off into a harbor, flying past a lighthouse, heading toward the sun.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: They say she's an ancestor of our family, from Portugal. That she was the first human to truly fly.
There was no question in Lucy's mind of who this mysterious woman had been. It was a remarkable likeness of the scene.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: I started this project in 1835 in Lisbon. Jimena and I made the first prototype of those wings.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: There was no engine in the first designs. We could only catch the wind.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: It was something of a bitter moment—I had to use my arcane skill to alter it so that Jimena could reach her ship. I never saw her again. I did not even know if she survived.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: I knew she had a partner, somehow, I never realized it was you.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: I spent a lot of time on other work after that. By the time I heard about your uncle's project, it had been 70 years.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: But still, we could not solve the problem of power. The technology just was not available to lift the frame for any significant length of time. He gave up.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: Did you know after he left Boston, Uncle Victor went to New York, made it rich with some olive oil business?

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: No, I never knew. But I am happy for him.
So, he achieved his goals after all. Just like Jimena did, in a way.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: He had always realized the business value of the wings.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: But he came to believe that it was impossible to achieve the design with the technology we had available.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: Humans have so little time, when you look at it. The future is always slipping out of their grasps.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: It is understandable why they grow frustrated after failing again and again. They do not have the time to wait around for the next miracle.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: But by handing down that ember, through you, he helped us get here. Now we've realized his dream, and Jimena's, and her father's before her.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: Yes, ideas, too, have a process of slow iteration.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: In the 19th century, only a few people even dreamed that humans would ever fly.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: In your uncle's time, it had already changed. People knew it was possible, but thought it would only ever be a novelty.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: Now, no one doubts where we can go.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: It is always only a matter of time, Joanna.
And time moves all, like a river. It cannot be stopped, and no one can control where it will take us.
No matter whether you rage against it, take every moment you can, or give up halfway.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: All that we need is patience.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: We will eventually get there, even though many of us may fall along the way.

items.speaker: Joanna
items.text: But you witnessed it all, Lucy. You kept that ember glowing.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: I just kept you company along the way.

items.speaker: Lucy
items.text: That is all I did.
